claim: Warner/Chappell collected licensing fees for Happy Birthday to You until a federal judge ruled in 2015 it held no valid copyright to the lyrics.
fact_check_evidence: Variety and NBC News (September 2015) report Judge George King ruled Warner/Chappell did not own a valid copyright in the Happy Birthday lyrics, in a suit by filmmakers over licensing fees. (https://variety.com/2015/biz/news/happy-birthday-song-public-domain-copyright-1201600319/ https://www.nbcnews.com/pop-culture/music/music-company-does-not-own-happy-birthday-song-copyright-judge-n432001)

claim: A musical work's copyright covers public performance, such as radio play; songwriters usually license it through organizations like ASCAP and BMI.
fact_check_evidence: The Copyright Office guide lists public performance (e.g. radio) among authors' rights and names ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR as PROs; Brookings notes songwriters receive performance royalties from terrestrial radio. (https://www.copyright.gov/music-modernization/educational-materials/musicians-income.pdf https://www.brookings.edu/opinions/why-artists-should-always-get-paid-by-broadcasters-who-play-their-songs/)

claim: In the US, the performance right for sound recordings covers only digital transmissions, so AM/FM radio pays no royalties for the recording itself.
fact_check_evidence: The Copyright Office musicians page says the sound-recording performance right is limited to digital audio transmissions; Brookings says performing artists and recording owners receive no royalties from terrestrial radio. (https://www.copyright.gov/engage/musicians/ https://www.brookings.edu/opinions/why-artists-should-always-get-paid-by-broadcasters-who-play-their-songs/)

claim: For 2026, the US statutory royalty for each song on a CD, vinyl record or download is 13.1 cents, or 2.52 cents a minute if that is larger.
fact_check_evidence: Digital Music News and Royalty Solutions report the Copyright Royalty Board set the 2026 physical and download mechanical rate at 13.1 cents or 2.52 cents per minute. (https://www.digitalmusicnews.com/2025/12/08/mechanical-royalty-rate-2026-adjustment-crb/ https://www.royaltysolutionscorp.com/blog/2026-mechanical-royalty-rate-increase)

claim: A 1993 study grouped Berlin music-academy violin students as best, good or future music teachers, and asked each to estimate their past practice.
fact_check_evidence: The Royal Society Open Science replication (2019) and the Purdue lab copy describe Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Romer's three groups at the Berlin academy and their retrospective practice estimates. (https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/6/8/190327/68523/The-role-of-deliberate-practice-in-expert https://mindsetonline.com/ericsson-deliberate-practice-violinists-berlin-10000-hours-wrong/)

claim: The best group reported about 7,400 hours of practice alone by age 18; the future music teachers about 3,400.
fact_check_evidence: Macnamara and Maitra (2019, PMC) report the 1993 estimates to age 18: about 7,410 hours for the best violinists and 3,420 for the music-teacher group. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6731745/ https://hhs.purdue.edu/skill-learning-and-performance-lab/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2024/08/macnamara-maitra-2019-the-role-of-deliberate-practice-in-expert-performance-revisiting-ericsson-krampe-tesch-romer.pdf)

claim: Deliberate practice is effortful work aimed at improving: well-defined tasks at the right difficulty, with informative feedback, unlike play.
fact_check_evidence: Ericsson and Harwell (2019) restate the 1993 definition: focused, effortful practice with the goal of improvement, well-defined tasks at an appropriate difficulty and informative feedback; ScienceDirect topic pages note it differs from play. (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02396/full https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/deliberate-practice)

claim: A 2014 meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained about 21% of the differences in music performance.
fact_check_evidence: The Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014) abstract and Frontiers commentary report 21% of variance explained for music. (https://scottbarrykaufman.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/Macnamara-et-al.-2014.pdf https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263713247_Deliberate_Practice_and_Performance_in_Music_Games_Sports_Education_and_Professions_A_Meta-Analysis)

claim: A 2019 repeat of the Berlin violin study found no significant practice difference between the best and good violinists.
fact_check_evidence: Royal Society Open Science (2019) abstract: the best and good violinists did not differ significantly in accumulated practice; Semantic Scholar summary agrees. (https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/6/8/190327/68523/The-role-of-deliberate-practice-in-expert https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/The-role-of-deliberate-practice-in-expert-Ericsson,-Macnamara-Maitra/2e9c716d2dab21bb634d87d62dadbb4176b2da53)

claim: Absolute pitch (perfect pitch) is the ability to name or produce a note without hearing a reference note.
fact_check_evidence: The Deutsch et al. (2006) PubMed abstract and Deutsch's Psychology of Music chapter define absolute pitch as naming or producing a note without a reference note. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16521731/ http://deutsch.ucsd.edu/pdf/PsyMus_3_Ch5_Absolute_Pitch.pdf)

claim: In the US and Europe, absolute pitch is estimated at fewer than 1 in 10,000 people.
fact_check_evidence: Deutsch et al. (2006) and their 2009 JASA follow-up cite a general-population prevalence of less than one in 10,000 (Profita and Bidder, 1988). (http://deutsch.ucsd.edu/pdf/JASA-2009_125_2398-2403.pdf https://www.researchgate.net/publication/24265523_Absolute_pitch_among_students_in_an_American_music_conservatory_Association_with_tone_language_fluency)

claim: Absolute pitch does not necessarily come with better performance on other musical tasks.
fact_check_evidence: Deutsch et al. (2006) cite several studies showing absolute pitch is not necessarily accompanied by superior processing on other musical tasks; Deutsch's review chapter says the same. (http://deutsch.ucsd.edu/pdf/PsyMus_3_Ch5_Absolute_Pitch.pdf http://deutsch.ucsd.edu/pdf/JASA-2006_119_719-722.pdf)

claim: Most people without absolute pitch still have surprisingly accurate long-term memory for pitch when they needn't name the note.
fact_check_evidence: Deutsch et al. (2006) cite Levitin (1994) and Deutsch et al. (1987): non-possessors show accurate long-term pitch memory when verbal labels are not required; Deutsch's review chapter discusses the same findings. (http://deutsch.ucsd.edu/pdf/PsyMus_3_Ch5_Absolute_Pitch.pdf https://deutsch.ucsd.edu/pdf/MP-2004-21_339-356.pdf)

claim: A 2006 study of conservatory students found more absolute pitch with earlier training, and far more among Mandarin speakers in Beijing than US students.
fact_check_evidence: The PubMed abstract of Deutsch et al. (2006): the earlier the onset of training the greater the prevalence, and prevalence far greater among Chinese (CCOM) than US (Eastman) students at each onset age. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16521731/ https://absolutepitch.org/studies/deutsch-2006.html)

claim: In Mandarin, a tone language, pitch changes meaning: ma can mean mother, hemp, horse or a reproach, depending on the tone.
fact_check_evidence: Deutsch et al. (2006) give the ma example; Deutsch's 2004 Music Perception paper and standard Mandarin references describe the same four-tone contrast. (https://deutsch.ucsd.edu/pdf/MP-2004-21_339-356.pdf https://ucsdguardian.org/2004/11/22/study-links-language-musical-ability/)

claim: Copland described three planes of listening: sensuous (the pleasure of the sound), expressive (feeling) and sheerly musical (the notes themselves).
fact_check_evidence: The excerpt names the sensuous, expressive and sheerly musical planes; secondary summaries (e.g. The Sublime blog, Writing Across Media wiki) describe the same three planes. (https://thesublimeblog.org/2021/07/19/aaron-copeland-how-we-listen/ https://wam.fandom.com/wiki/Aaron_Copland_%22How_We_Listen%22)

claim: Copland wrote that casual listeners notice melody first, then rhythm, and take harmony and tone color for granted.
fact_check_evidence: Direct text of the excerpt ("How We Listen"): melody is mentioned first, rhythm next, while harmony and tone color are generally taken for granted; the Hunter College (CUNY) copy of the essay carries the same passage. (https://springmuse.hunter.cuny.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Copland-How-We-Listen-To-Music.pdf https://thesublimeblog.org/2021/07/19/aaron-copeland-how-we-listen/)

claim: Copland said we really listen on all three planes at once, and urged being someone who is listening for something.
fact_check_evidence: The excerpt says we listen in all three ways at the same time and ends by urging readers to be "listening for something"; the Hunter College (CUNY) copy of the essay carries the same text. (https://springmuse.hunter.cuny.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Copland-How-We-Listen-To-Music.pdf https://thesublimeblog.org/2021/07/19/aaron-copeland-how-we-listen/)

claim: WHO says 80 dB is safe for up to 40 hours a week, but at 90 dB safe listening time drops to four hours a week.
fact_check_evidence: The WHO safe-listening Q&A states both limits; the WHO Make Listening Safe materials and Hearing Health Foundation cite the same. (https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/deafness-and-hearing-loss-safe-listening https://hearinghealthfoundation.org/keeplistening/decibels)

claim: WHO advises keeping a personal audio device at no more than 60% of its maximum volume.
fact_check_evidence: The WHO safe-listening Q&A recommends setting device volume to no more than 60% of maximum; the American Tinnitus Association repeats the WHO advice. (https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/deafness-and-hearing-loss-safe-listening https://www.ata.org/protecting-young-people-from-noise-induced-hearing-loss/)

claim: Human hair cells in the inner ear do not grow back once destroyed, but noise-induced hearing loss is completely preventable.
fact_check_evidence: The NIDCD noise-induced hearing loss page states human hair cells don't grow back and NIHL is the only completely preventable type; WHO says the resulting damage is permanent. (https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/noise-induced-hearing-loss https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/deafness-and-hearing-loss-safe-listening)
